title: Optimal quantum discrimination at Liouvillian exceptional points
abstract: Central to non-Hermitian sensing is the question of whether exceptional points (EPs) can make weak perturbations easier to detect. We show that despite enhanced spectral response, in finite-dimensional Lindblad systems with a unique stationary state and a nonzero relaxation gap, EPs offer no fundamental advantage in how the observation time required for reliable detection of a weak perturbation scales with the perturbation strength. We nevertheless demonstrate that by selectively choosing perturbations that enhance the quantum Fisher information rate, EPs can shorten the observation time needed to reach a predefined detection accuracy relative to a comparable non-EP reference at the same decay rate. As an illustration, we show using an optomechanical model at an EP that we can detect a weak force through the cavity output at the same reliability in less time than a non-EP reference. Our results establish fundamental limits on perturbation detection at EPs and can guide the design of faster non-Hermitian sensors based on optomechanical resonators, superconducting qubits, and trapped ions.
summary: This paper analyzes the fundamental limits of quantum sensing near Exceptional Points (EPs) in open quantum systems. It shows that while EPs don't fundamentally alter the scaling of detection time, they allow for a significant reduction in observation time compared to non-EP systems by selectively enhancing the Quantum Fisher Information rate. The analysis is demonstrated using a detailed optomechanical model.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether operating an open quantum system at an Exceptional Point (EP) provides a fundamental advantage in the observation time required for reliably detecting a weak external perturbation compared to a standard non-EP reference.
main_result: While EPs do not fundamentally change the scaling of detection time with perturbation strength ($\delta$), they can significantly shorten the required observation time for a fixed detection accuracy by selectively enhancing the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) rate.
method: The analysis uses quantum discrimination theory, calculating the detection probability via the state overlap and deriving the required observation time from the growth rate of the QFI, comparing EP dynamics to non-EP dynamics.
model_or_system: The study models finite-dimensional Markovian open quantum systems governed by a Lindblad generator. A specific illustration uses an optomechanical system involving cavity and mechanical oscillators.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) rate ($f_Q$), state overlap ($A_T$), and the required observation time ($T_{	ext{disc}}$) for a target detection probability ($p$).
important_parameters: Perturbation strength ($\delta$), observation time ($T$), and system parameters defining the EP structure (e.g., $\eta, u, \Gamma$).
main_assumptions: The general analysis assumes finite-dimensional Markovian open systems with a unique stationary state and a nonzero relaxation gap. The numerical examples rely on the weak perturbation limit ($\epsilon \ll \Gamma$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the separation of timescales, showing that the required detection time ($T_{	ext{disc}} \sim |\delta|^{-2}$) is much longer than the EP splitting time ($T_{	ext{split}} \sim |\delta|^{-1/m}$). Figure 2(b) shows the time advantage in the optomechanical case.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general detection limit for weak perturbations at EPs. It then derives the scaling law for the required detection time. Finally, it applies these concepts to the optomechanical model to quantify the time advantage gained by tuning the perturbation to enhance the QFI rate.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical utility of non-Hermitian physics in sensing, providing quantitative guidelines for designing faster, more sensitive quantum sensors using platforms like optomechanics and superconducting qubits.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Separation of timescales. For the finite-dimensional gapped Lindblad systems, a generic perturbation δ of an EP of order m, the best probability P of correctly deciding whether it is present approaches 50% on the inverse-splitting timescale as δ →0. Presence and absence are equally likely. Reliable detection requires much longer observation times.

FIG. 2: Finite improvements in EP-based detection. (a) For a single real EP2 decay block, the most- and least-informative perturbation directions have relative information rates E± = 1 ± ε, with 0 < ε ≤1; the illustration uses ε = 1/2. (b) For a selected weak mechanical force and ideal collection of the cavity emission (η = 1), the optomechanical EP sensor reaches a 90% probability of a correct decision with 49.85% less observation time than a non-EP reference oscillator with the same decay rate. The curves show the weak-force limit and the time is normalized to the reference oscillator’s time to reach the same 90% target.
